analysis.title: "We Know Where The Pain Trade Lies": Goldman Sees Squeeze In Under-Owned Europe, Russell As Bond Vol Finally Blinks
key_insights: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky (EMEA head of delta-one trading) says rates are finding their feet after a volatile week. Treasury auctions were relatively well absorbed and longer-dated bond vol retraced roughly 30% of its recent move.

Privorotsky's scenario: bond vol compresses, yields stay high but stabilize, and the drag on the rest of the economy eases. Speculators are heavily short bonds and Russell and long Nasdaq, so the pain trade is a calm bond market. He sees headline indices treading water while under-owned Europe and the Russell outperform.
US fundamental long/short net leverage rose 0.5 points to 46.9% last week, still the 2nd percentile of the past year. The S&P is near all-time highs while hedge fund net exposure is near its lows.

Goldman's US Equity Sentiment Indicator (nine measures of institutional, retail and foreign positioning) is at -1.3 standard deviations, below the -1.0 'light positioning' threshold. Privorotsky: 'Still a ton of capacity.'

Pasquariello says the trading community 'carries a conspicuously low level of length.' John Flood says the 'perfect recipe' (buybacks, negative sentiment, low HF nets, supercap IPOs, big earnings season) could take the S&P through 8,000 in short order. Consensus Q3 EPS growth is 27% y/y.

US hedge funds rotated into Industrials and out of Info Tech last week. Info Tech had been the most-bought sector in 4 of the prior 5 weeks and was the most net sold at -1.0 SD. Selling was heaviest on Oct 8, when the FT reported disappointing OpenAI revenues and the Nasdaq fell.

Privorotsky sees the OpenAI headline as largely an accounting-definition question. He reads the reaction as evidence of more length and rising sensitivity in those pockets. Goldman's flow team says the headline 'brought out significant semis and tech supply,' which points to nervous or forced length.
Hedge fund gross leverage rose 3.8 points to 213% (80th percentile on a 3-year view). Net is in the low single-digit percentiles and the long/short ratio is at 0% of its 1-year range.

Russell 2000 futures positioning is at record shorts and IWM short interest is at a record high, yet IWM implied vol is below the 10th percentile. Small-cap upside calls are cheap relative to the short base, and the desk saw demand for small-cap calls last week.

Small caps are a rates trade: Russell underperformed Nasdaq in 17 of the last 20 sessions. If long-end vol keeps falling, rate-sensitive small caps should benefit first and the record short base becomes forced buying.
Garrett calls 2026 the most dispersive calendar year in history. The realized vol spread between the average stock and the index is about 27 over three months.

Privorotsky calls Europe 'suddenly under owned.' Catalysts: the Oct 12 EU/China hybrid agreement (targets about a 50% cut in projected Chinese hybrid imports, positive for European autos and a catalyst for a momentum unwind), calmer OATs, and perceived progress on Russia/Ukraine after an energy ceasefire.
Goldman CTA estimates show trend-followers hold about $10B of European equities versus about $40B of US equities (chart-read, approximate), which leaves room for a catch-up trade.
Louis Miller says AI versus everything else hit a record 10-point gap in five weeks (Oct 11) and argues for starting to buy the losers.

Risks: Brent is about $103 and the energy shock's underlying problem is unresolved. Privorotsky wanted a 'more durable off ramp by now' and calls the index setup 'more like a chop at the highs/consolidation.'

Calendar: Tuesday bank earnings start, Wednesday CPI (consensus 0.6% headline, 0.2% core) and ASML, Thursday TSMC plus PPI and retail sales, Friday Warsh. Privorotsky says a 10bp downside surprise in core CPI would be meaningful for rates.

The author's caveat: AI-related issuance competes with Treasuries for duration buyers, 30-year yields hit their highest since 2002 last week, and France's bond rout was only 'contained'. The 30% retracement in bond vol is a pause, so the squeeze is likely to be a rental rather than a lasting trend.

tension_points.bull_case: Bond vol has retraced about 30%, auctions were well absorbed, and positioning is lopsided (record Russell shorts, 2nd-percentile HF net, CTAs light in Europe). Calm bonds would force a squeeze in the Russell and Europe.
tension_points.bear_case: The retracement is a pause. 30-year yields hit their highest since 2002, AI-related issuance competes for duration buyers, France's bond rout is only contained, and Brent is around $103.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A hot Wednesday CPI print (consensus 0.6% headline, 0.2% core) or a renewed rise in long-end bond vol.
